You must produce:

Instructions

• For related work and baselines:

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
In the field of visual neural decoding, recent approaches aim to retrieve or reconstruct original visual stimuli by directly aligning encoded brain signals (such as EEG, MEG, or fMRI) with pretrained image representations via contrastive learning. However, this direct alignment ignores two fundamental discrepancies between digital images and human brain activity:
1. **The System Gap:** The human visual and cognitive systems cannot process or memorize all details of a visual stimulus. Due to biological constraints—such as the rapid drop-off in visual resolution outside the fovea and limits in working memory—high-frequency visual details are inevitably lost when an image is translated into a brain signal. 
2. **The Random Gap:** Human perception and cognition are highly dynamic. Shifting attention, wandering thoughts, and biological or technical noise during signal acquisition create heavy stochastic variability in brain responses, even when viewing the exact same stimulus.

Because of these inherent gaps, perfect alignment between pristine digital images and noisy, lossy brain signals is impossible. When models attempt to forcefully bridge these gaps using limited paired datasets, they severely overfit to the training data, leading to poor generalization on new, unseen signals. 

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that instead of forcing a neural network to hallucinate missing high-frequency details from noisy brain signals, we should proactively degrade the target visual stimuli to match the biological and technical constraints of the brain data. 

We hypothesize that by introducing a biologically-inspired "blur prior" to the images—and dynamically adjusting the intensity of this blur based on the estimated uncertainty (noise) of each specific brain-image pair—we can artificially close the System and Random gaps. This will prevent the contrastive learning model from overfitting to unlearnable high-frequency details and fundamentally improve multimodal alignment.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We will develop an **Uncertainty-Aware Blur Prior** framework built on top of a standard multi-modal contrastive learning architecture. The approach involves three core logical steps:

**1. Vision-Brain Contrastive Base Pipeline**
We will utilize a dual-encoder setup consisting of a trainable brain signal encoder and a frozen, pretrained vision encoder. The objective is to map both modalities into a shared latent space where matching brain-image pairs are pulled together and non-matching pairs are pushed apart using a symmetric cross-entropy strategy.

**2. Simulating Biological Vision (The Blur Prior)**
To address the "System Gap," we will apply a specialized spatial transformation to the input images before they are passed to the vision encoder. Inspired by the human visual system, we will generate a foveated blur effect. By applying a distance-based blending mechanism, we will keep the center of the image relatively sharp while progressively blurring the peripheral regions. This step conceptually acts as a low-pass filter, stripping away the high-frequency visual details that the human brain fails to encode, thereby establishing a more biologically realistic target for the brain encoder.

**3. Dynamic Uncertainty Quantification and Adaptive Blurring**
To address the "Random Gap" (stochastic noise and shifting attention), we will make the blur prior dynamic. Since we cannot easily separate cognitive noise from technical noise, we will track the alignment similarity scores of the paired samples in the latent space during training. 
* We will treat the distribution of these similarity scores as a proxy for signal-to-noise ratio. 
* We will establish a moving statistical confidence interval over these similarities. 
* If a paired sample falls outside this expected interval, we will flag it as a highly uncertain, mismatched pair (indicating a large Random Gap).
* For these highly uncertain pairs, we will dynamically increase the radius of the foveated blur applied to the image. Conversely, for well-aligned pairs, we will apply a milder blur. 

By modulating the image degradation on a per-sample basis, the model will intelligently back off from trying to learn high-frequency mappings when the underlying brain signal is excessively noisy.

## Expected Contribution
This approach will offer a conceptually novel way to handle noisy, mismatched modalities in brain-computer interfaces. By explicitly modeling the biological limits of human vision and the stochastic uncertainty of brain signals, we expect to provide a robust regularization mechanism that prevents overfitting in multimodal contrastive learning. Ultimately, this will yield highly generalized brain-to-image retrieval and decoding models that remain stable even when deployed across subjects with highly variable or noisy neural responses.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

* **Datasets:**
  * **THINGS-EEG:** A large-scale Electroencephalogram (EEG) dataset consisting of 10 subjects utilizing the Rapid Serial Visual Presentation (RSVP) paradigm. 
    * *Training Set:* 1,654 concepts with 10 images per concept. Each image was repeated 4 times per subject. Repetitions were averaged to achieve a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), yielding 16,540 training samples per subject.
    * *Test Set:* 200 concepts with 1 image per concept. Each image was repeated 80 times per subject. Repetitions were averaged, yielding 200 test samples per subject.
  * **THINGS-MEG:** A Magnetoencephalography (MEG) dataset involving 4 participants and 271 channels.
    * *Training Set:* 1,854 concepts, 12 images per concept, 1 repetition per image.
    * *Test Set:* 200 concepts, 1 image per concept, 12 repetitions per image. Repetitions of the same stimulus were averaged to ensure SNR.
* **Evaluation Metrics:**
  * Zero-shot brain-to-image retrieval task: Top-1 Accuracy (%) and Top-5 Accuracy (%).
  * Additional metrics monitored: Mean Average Precision (mAP), Similarity Score, Pearson correlation, and Spearman correlation (for evaluating robustness to subject variability).
* **Baselines Compared:**
  * BraVL (Mixture of Experts model based on multimodal brain-visual-linguistic features)
  * NICE (Self-supervised framework with self-attention spatial modules)
  * NICE-SA (Self-attention variant)
  * NICE-GA (Graph attention variant)
  * ATM-S (Adaptive Thinking Mapper incorporating position and temporospatial encoding)
  * VE-SDN (Visual-EEG Semantic Decouple Framework)
* **Implementation Details:**
  * **Brain Encoders:** Evaluated multiple architectures to ensure generalizability. The default was *EEGProject* (comprising two linear layers with residual connections and a normalization layer). Other evaluated architectures included Shallownet, Deepnet, EEGnet, and TSconv.
  * **Vision Encoders:** Utilized the visual branches of pretrained vision-language contrastive models. The default was *RN50*. Other evaluated architectures included RN101, ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14, ViT-H/14, ViT-g/14, and ViT-bigG/14.
  * **Methodology (Uncertainty-aware Blur Prior - UBP):** 
    * We aligned encoded representations of brain signals with visual stimuli embeddings using a symmetric cross-entropy (SCE) loss.
    * To mitigate the "System GAP" (inherent loss of high-frequency visual details during human processing), we applied dynamic Gaussian blurring to visual stimuli.
    * We synthesized foveated blur images to simulate human macular and peripheral vision regions.
    * To mitigate the "Random GAP" (variability induced by dynamic perception/cognition and technical noise), we utilized an uncertainty quantification mechanism.
    * We calculated multi-modal similarity scores across pairs, maintaining a moving average during iterations. Because paired-sample similarity followed a Gaussian distribution, we defined a confidence interval. Pairs falling outside this confidence interval had their blur radius ($r$) dynamically adjusted (increased for outliers indicating high discrepancy).

## 3. Qualitative Observations

* **Information Flow and GAPs:** During the evaluation of the Rapid Serial Visual Presentation (RSVP) paradigm, we identified distinct information bottlenecks. We observed a "System GAP" transitioning from raw visual stimuli to human perception, inherently characterized by the loss of high-frequency visual details. We also identified a "Random GAP" occurring between cognition and the final collected brain signal. This Random GAP was driven by three primary factors: 1) dynamic shifts in visual attention, 2) dynamic associative cognition over identical images, and 3) low-level technical noise during signal acquisition.
* **Brain Signal Clustering and Subject Variability:** When analyzing the EEG signals over 80 trials, we observed significant variance even when tracking identical stimuli. UMAP projections of EEG data across 10 subjects yielded highly distinct subject-specific clustering patterns, emphasizing large inter-subject variability. Furthermore, when computing the density distribution of EEG variability, we observed that higher variability in a subject's signals negatively correlated with overall retrieval performance.
* **Similarity Distribution and Uncertainty Areas:** By calculating a semantic similarity matrix between image features and corresponding EEG features, we observed that the multi-modal similarity scores across matched pairs approximately followed a normal distribution. Using this, we established statistical confidence intervals. Similarity scores that dropped outside the interval thresholds (the "Uncertainty Area") reliably flagged poorly aligned samples suffering from extreme "Random GAP" degradation.
* **Impact of Data Transformations on the System GAP:** We tested numerous data augmentations and corruptions to analyze their effect on the System GAP. We observed that transformations restricted to altering geometric configurations or global color distributions (e.g., flipping, cropping, grayscale, color jitter) yielded minimal retrieval improvements. Conversely, corruptive techniques that aggressively degraded high-frequency image details (e.g., Gaussian noise, lowering resolution, applying uniform blur, and fovea blur) dramatically increased retrieval performance. Fovea blur specifically produced the strongest static improvement, closely mimicking human optical distortion. 
* **Dynamic Blurring and Optimal Blur Radius:** When conducting sensitivity analysis across various uniform blur radii (ranging from 0 to 41), we observed a parabolic impact on model accuracy. As blur radius increased from 0, both Top-1 and Top-5 accuracy strictly increased, peaking optimally at a blur radius of 11. Increasing the radius further induced a decline in performance. At a radius of 41, the excessive loss of information pushed accuracy below the un-blurred baseline. Ultimately, integrating dynamic blurring driven by uncertainty scores (UBP) out-performed all static augmentation configurations.
* **Validating Uncertainty Estimation using Non-Averaged Trials:** To empirically validate whether our uncertainty boundaries successfully isolated poor signals, we compared the similarity score distributions of standard averaged EEG trials versus raw, non-averaged EEG trials (serving as proxies for low SNR / high-mismatch outliers). We observed that the vast majority of non-averaged samples fell squarely outside the confidence interval of the averaged samples, verifying the efficacy of identifying "Random GAP" impacts via interval exclusion.
* **Robustness Across Model Architectures:** In our comprehensive ablation study crossing five discrete brain encoders with eight separate vision encoders, we observed consistent performance gains. Our proposed Uncertainty-aware Blur Prior reliably improved Top-1 accuracy over the baselines in every single encoder pairing, indicating the method operates independently of specific model architectures.
* **Robustness to Subject Variability:** We observed that prior baseline systems (e.g., NICE-SA, VE-SDN, and vanilla implementations) exhibited extreme sensitivity to subject signal variability, evidenced by starkly negative Pearson correlation scores between subject variance and Top-1 accuracy (e.g., -0.783 for NICE-SA). In contrast, our proposed approach demonstrated significant robustness to this variability, yielding a much flatter correlation (-0.481) and retaining reliable performance even on highly variable subjects.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts

references.text:
## Problem Statement

To understand the mechanisms between human vision and brain activity, neural decoding methods aim to retrieve and reconstruct original visual stimuli by aligning the representations of brain signals with visual stimuli. However, existing methods fundamentally fail to account for two critical discrepancies between digital image modalities and brain signal modalities, leading to severe overfitting and poor generalization:

1.  **The System GAP:** The human visual system cannot process and retain all visual information due to constrained attentional resources, finite working memory, and physiological limitations (e.g., non-uniform visual resolution that degrades from the fovea toward the periphery). Consequently, high-frequency details from the original visual stimuli are unavoidably lost when transformed into brain signals.
2.  **The Random GAP:** The fidelity of brain signals is further degraded by stochastic factors, including dynamic shifts in perceptual attention, cognitive associations, and low-level technical noise during signal acquisition (e.g., poor electrode contact). This variability induces an extreme information mismatch, severely lowering the signal-to-noise ratio.

Directly aligning encoded brain representations with corresponding pretrained high-fidelity image features forces models to bridge these unbridgeable gaps. Because paired multi-modal data is notoriously scarce, the network overfits to the mismatch rather than learning generalizable semantic mappings.

## Core Hypothesis

We propose the **Uncertainty-aware Blur Prior (UBP)** framework. We hypothesize that we can synthetically bridge the System GAP by injecting a biological prior—dynamically blurring high-frequency details of the visual stimuli to simulate the human visual field's peripheral degradation. Furthermore, to address the Random GAP, we hypothesize that the similarity distribution of multi-modal sample pairs can serve as a proxy for alignment uncertainty. By quantifying this uncertainty, we can dynamically adjust the severity of the blur prior on a per-sample basis. This will effectively mask out the noisy, mismatched high-frequency features in the visual modality, preventing the model from overfitting to the GAPs and significantly boosting the generalization of the shared latent space.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Notation and Shared Latent Space Definition
We will operate on paired multi-modal data $(x_v, x_b) \sim P_M$, where $x_v \in \mathbb{R}^{d_V}$ represents an image from the visual domain distribution $P_V$, and $x_b \in \mathbb{R}^{d_B}$ represents the corresponding brain signal from distribution $P_B$.

The primary objective is to map the brain data to a $k$-dimensional shared latent space $\mathcal{H} \in \mathbb{R}^k$. We will utilize a frozen visual encoder $f_V: \mathcal{X}_V \to \mathcal{H}$ (specifically, the visual branch of a pretrained Contrastive Vision-Language model, such as ResNet-50) to extract visual embeddings. We will architect and train a brain encoder $f_B: \mathcal{X}_B \to \mathcal{H}$ parameterized by $\omega$. The architecture of $f_B$ will consist of two linear layers connected via a residual pathway, followed by a normalization layer.

### 2. Vision-Brain Contrastive Learning Objective
Given a positive multi-modal pair $(x_v, x_b)$ and independent negative samples $x_v^\prime \sim P_V$ and $x_b^\prime \sim P_B$, our encoders yield the latent representations $(h_v, h_b, h_v^\prime, h_b^\prime)$. We will optimize the parameters $\omega$ of $f_B$ using a Symmetric Cross-Entropy (SCE) loss, defined as:

$$ \mathcal{L}_{SCE}(f_B) = - \mathbb{E}_{x_v, x_b} \log \frac{\exp(f_V(x_v) \cdot f_B(x_b) / \tau)}{\mathbb{E}_{x_b^\prime} \exp(f_V(x_v) \cdot f_B(x_b^\prime) / \tau)} - \mathbb{E}_{x_v, x_b} \log \frac{\exp(f_V(x_v) \cdot f_B(x_b) / \tau)}{\mathbb{E}_{x_v^\prime} \exp(f_V(x_v^\prime) \cdot f_B(x_b) / \tau)} $$

where $\tau$ is the temperature parameter regulating the scale of the logits.

### 3. Foveated Blur Prior Construction (Addressing System GAP)
To mitigate the model's tendency to overfit to unperceived high-frequency details, we will synthesize a foveated blur effect on the input image $x_v$. 

First, we generate a uniformly blurred image $x_{blur}$ using a Gaussian kernel of radius $r = 2k + 1$:

$$ x_{blur}(i, j) = \sum_{m=-k}^{k} \sum_{n=-k}^{k} x(i - m, j - n) \cdot G(m,n) $$

where $x(i-m, j-n)$ is the pixel value in the original image, and $G(m,n)$ represents the Gaussian kernel weights defined by:

$$ G(m,n) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2} \exp\left(-\frac{m^2 + n^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) $$

where $\sigma$ is the standard deviation controlling blur intensity. 

We will then blend the original and blurred images to simulate foveal vision:

$$ \tilde{x}_v = \alpha \cdot x + (1 - \alpha) \cdot x_{blur} $$

where $\alpha$ is a spatial blending factor matrix ($0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$). To simulate peripheral degradation, $\alpha$ decays exponentially based on the distance from the fovea (the center of the image):

$$ \alpha(i, j) = \exp \left( - \lambda \cdot \frac{d(i, j)}{L} \right) $$

Here, $d(i, j)$ is the Euclidean distance from pixel $(i, j)$ to the fovea, $L$ is the maximum possible distance within the image, and $\lambda$ is a hyperparameter controlling the rate of peripheral decay.

### 4. Uncertainty Quantification and Dynamic Alignment (Addressing Random GAP)
Because the Random GAP is highly stochastic, we will estimate multi-modal uncertainty dynamically during training to adjust the blur radius $r$. For a batch of $N$ paired samples $\{(x_v^i, x_b^i)\}_{i=1}^N$, we process the blurred images to obtain latents $h_v \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$ and $h_b \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$. 

We compute the pair-wise similarity matrix $M \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}$ as:

$$ M = h_b \cdot h_v^\top \cdot \text{softplus}(\theta) $$

where $\theta$ is a learned scalar parameter, and the $\text{softplus}$ activation ensures positivity. The diagonal of this matrix represents the similarity scores for the positive pairs, denoted as $S = \text{diag}(M) \in \mathbb{R}^N$. To maintain temporal smoothness, we will apply a moving average to $M$ across training iterations.

Assuming the similarity scores $S$ follow a normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(\hat{\mu}, \hat{\sigma}^2)$, we calculate the batch mean and variance:

$$ \hat{\mu} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N S_i, \quad \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{N-1} \sum_{i=1}^N (S_i - \hat{\mu})^2 $$

We establish a confidence interval for the similarity scores at a confidence level of $1-\gamma$:

$$ \left[ \hat{\mu} - z_{\gamma/2} \cdot \hat{\sigma}, \quad \hat{\mu} + z_{\gamma/2} \cdot \hat{\sigma} \right] $$

where $z_{\gamma/2}$ is the critical value from the standard normal distribution. Pairs falling outside this interval indicate severe Random GAP mismatch (high uncertainty). Based on the similarity score $s$ of a given pair, we dynamically update its target blur radius $r(s)$ for the next iteration:

$$ r(s) = \begin{cases} 
r_0 - c, & \text{if } s < \hat{\mu} - z_{\gamma/2} \cdot \hat{\sigma} \\ 
r_0 + c, & \text{if } s > \hat{\mu} + z_{\gamma/2} \cdot \hat{\sigma} \\ 
r_0, & \text{if } \hat{\mu} - z_{\gamma/2} \cdot \hat{\sigma} \leq s \leq \hat{\mu} + z_{\gamma/2} \cdot \hat{\sigma} 
\end{cases} $$

where $r_0$ is the baseline blur radius and $c$ is a step constant. A larger discrepancy triggers greater blurring to destroy uncorroborated high-frequency details, while confident pairs receive milder blurring.

## Expected Contribution

This proposal outlines the first visual neural decoding architecture to explicitly model and compensate for the physiological limitations of human vision and the stochastic noise of cognitive dynamics. By integrating a biologically-inspired foveated prior with dynamic, uncertainty-driven representation scaling, the proposed method theoretically eliminates multi-modal overfitting caused by the System and Random GAPs. We anticipate that this architecture will yield highly robust, subject-agnostic latent alignments, maximizing zero-shot retrieval accuracy without requiring perfectly clean or high-density neural recordings.

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no coding agent: a 23-stage prompt-chain pipeline over the Anthropic Messages API

network.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).

tools.permissions: no tool calls (requests carry model, messages, max_tokens); generated experiments run as plain subprocesses in the container

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
